questions.question: What is the difference between String, StringBuilder, and StringBuffer in Java?
questions.title: String vs StringBuilder vs StringBuffer
questions.direct_answer: String is immutable — every modification creates a new object. StringBuilder is a mutable buffer optimized for single-threaded string construction. StringBuffer is identical to StringBuilder but every method is synchronized, making it thread-safe at the cost of performance. In modern code StringBuilder is nearly always the right choice for dynamic string assembly.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand immutability and its implications, when mutation matters for performance, and whether you know that StringBuffer's synchronization is rarely needed
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Recommending StringBuffer for thread-safety without realizing that compound operations (append + append) still aren't atomic, or not knowing that the compiler converts simple string concatenation to StringBuilder internally
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that the Java compiler rewrites `+` concatenation to StringBuilder for single-expression concatenation, but a loop with `+` still creates O(n) intermediate Strings. Mention Java 15+ text blocks and that Java 9+ uses StringConcatFactory for even better inlining.

sections.title: Why Every concat() Allocates a New Object — and Why That's Usually Fine
sections.content:
Most developers think the choice between String, StringBuilder, and StringBuffer is about performance. It isn't — it's about **mutability**, and everything else follows from that single property.

String is backed by a `final byte[]` that cannot change after construction. Every method that appears to modify a String — `concat()`, `replace()`, `toUpperCase()` — actually allocates a brand-new String and copies the characters. The original is untouched. This immutability is what makes String safe to share across threads without synchronization, safe to use as a HashMap key without worrying about hash corruption, and eligible for the JVM's **string pool** where `"hello" == "hello"` is literally true.

StringBuilder and StringBuffer both extend `AbstractStringBuilder`, which holds a **mutable** `byte[]` with a separate length counter. `append()` writes directly into the buffer, growing it by doubling when it runs out of space. No new object per operation — just pointer advancement. The only difference between the two is that StringBuffer wraps every method in `synchronized`, while StringBuilder does not.

The misconception worth correcting: StringBuffer's per-method synchronization **doesn't make compound operations atomic**. `buffer.append(x).append(y)` is two separate lock acquisitions — another thread can interleave between them. You pay the locking cost without getting real thread safety for any realistic use case.

sections.title: Immutability, Thread Safety, and Performance: What Actually Differs
sections.content:
The table reveals that the three classes differ on exactly **two axes** — mutability and synchronization — and everything else is a consequence of those two properties.

| Feature | String | StringBuilder | StringBuffer |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mutable | No — `final byte[]` | Yes — mutable buffer | Yes — mutable buffer |
| Thread-safe | Yes (immutable = inherently safe) | No — no synchronization | Per-method `synchronized` |
| Performance (single thread) | Creates new object per change | Fastest — no locking overhead | Slower — acquires lock on every call |
| String pool eligible | Yes — literals are pooled and deduplicated | No | No |
| Safe as HashMap key | Yes — hash value can be cached and never changes | No — mutation would corrupt bucket placement | No — same problem |
| Compound operation safety | N/A (immutable) | Not thread-safe | Still not atomic — `append(x).append(y)` is two locks |
| Use case | Values, constants, keys, interned strings | Building strings in loops or dynamic assembly | Legacy APIs — virtually never needed in modern code |

The **compound operation row** is the one that matters most for interviews. Candidates who recommend StringBuffer for thread safety miss that `buffer.append(a).append(b)` releases the lock between the two appends. Another thread can sneak in between them, producing garbled output. If you genuinely need thread-safe string building, wrap a `StringBuilder` in an explicit `synchronized` block — at least the scope of the lock is visible and covers the full operation.

sections.title: The Loop Trap: Where the Compiler Can't Save You
Key Points
sections.content:
- **String is immutable** — every modification allocates a brand-new object; immutability makes it thread-safe and poolable.
- **`+` in loops is O(n squared)** — compiler rewrites single-expression `+` to `StringBuilder`; only explicit `StringBuilder` helps in loops.
- **StringBuilder is mutable, not thread-safe** — amortized O(1) append; call `toString()` at the end.
- **StringBuffer is synchronized but misleading** — `buffer.append(x).append(y)` acquires the lock twice; another thread can interleave between.
- **No valid modern use case for StringBuffer** — use `StringBuilder` for single-threaded string building.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The distinction comes down to mutability — String is immutable, StringBuilder is mutable, and StringBuffer is the synchronized but rarely-needed legacy version.

**String:**
- Every modification (`concat()`, `replace()`, `+`) allocates a brand-new object
- Immutability makes it thread-safe, poolable, and safe as a HashMap key
- The compiler rewrites single-expression `+` to `StringBuilder` (Java 9+: `StringConcatFactory`)

**StringBuilder:**
- Mutable internal buffer — no allocations until `toString()`
- Use explicitly in loops: `result += row` is O(n²), `sb.append(row)` is O(n)
- Not thread-safe — safe for single-threaded use only

**StringBuffer:**
- Synchronized version of StringBuilder — every method acquires a lock
- The synchronization is misleading: `buffer.append(x).append(y)` acquires and releases the lock twice — another thread can interleave between them
- No valid modern use case — StringBuilder is always better single-threaded

I recommend String for literals and simple concatenation, StringBuilder for building in loops, and ignoring StringBuffer.

questions.question: Explain the Java String pool, how interning works, and when to use or avoid it.
questions.title: String Pool and Interning
questions.direct_answer: The String pool (string intern table) is a special heap region (since Java 7, in the main heap; before that, in PermGen) where string literals are deduplicated. When the JVM encounters a string literal, it checks the pool first. String.intern() manually places a string into the pool and returns the canonical reference. Two interned strings can then be compared with == instead of equals().

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand heap vs pool, PermGen vs heap evolution, and the performance trade-offs of intern().
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking the pool is in PermGen in all Java versions. Since Java 7, it moved to the main heap and is GC-eligible.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss G1 GC's String Deduplication feature (-XX:+UseStringDeduplication) as an automatic alternative to manual interning.

sections.title: Why "hello" == "hello" Is True — and Why That's a Feature, Not a Bug
sections.content:
A typical enterprise Java application uses thousands of string literals — `"GET"`, `"Content-Type"`, `"id"`, `"null"`. If the JVM allocated a fresh heap object every time it encountered the same literal, these identical character sequences would consume enormous memory for zero benefit.

The **string pool** (also called the intern table) is the JVM's deduplication solution. When a class is loaded and the JVM encounters the literal `"hello"`, it checks the pool first. If an entry with the same content already exists, it returns the existing reference. If not, it adds the string and returns the new entry. This is why `"hello" == "hello"` is `true` — both references point to the exact same pool object, not two equal-but-separate objects.

Strings created via `new String("hello")` deliberately bypass the pool and land on the regular heap as independent objects. That's why `new String("hello") == "hello"` is `false` even though `.equals()` returns `true`. The `String.intern()` method is the manual bridge: call it on any heap string and you get back the canonical pooled reference, creating one if it doesn't exist yet.

The interesting part isn't how the pool works — it's where it lives, what happens when it grows, and when `intern()` helps versus when it just adds locking overhead.

sections.title: The PermGen Trap: Why Interning Could Crash Pre-Java-7 Applications
sections.content:
Before Java 7, the string pool lived in **PermGen** (Permanent Generation) — a fixed-size memory region outside the regular heap that was not subject to normal garbage collection. PermGen was sized via `-XX:MaxPermSize`, typically 64–256 MB.

This design had a critical flaw. Interned strings in PermGen were **never garbage collected** — even when no live references remained, the pool entry stayed forever. For long-running services that interned user-provided strings (parsed CSV values, dynamic keys), this was a slow, unstoppable memory leak that only ended with a JVM restart.

Web applications suffered most. Each hot-redeploy loaded a fresh classloader with fresh string literals. The old classloader's strings couldn't be reclaimed because PermGen GC was unreliable. After enough redeploys, the application threw `OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space` — a cryptic error that didn't point to any application code because the root cause was in JVM memory management. Teams learned to schedule periodic JVM restarts as a workaround, which is the kind of operational hack that signals a design problem.

sections.title: Java 7 Moved the Pool to the Heap — Making Interned Strings GC-Eligible
sections.content:
Java 7 relocated the string pool from PermGen to the **main heap**, which fixed both problems in one move. Pooled strings now participate in normal garbage collection — when no live references to a pooled string remain, the GC reclaims it like any other heap object. The `OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space` error for string-heavy applications effectively disappeared.

The pool itself is implemented as a **native hash table** inside the JVM, with a configurable bucket count. The defaults grew across versions: Java 7 started around 1,009 buckets, Java 11 uses roughly 65,536, and Java 17+ defaults to approximately 1 million. If your application interns a large number of distinct strings and `intern()` calls slow down, `-XX:StringTableSize` lets you increase the bucket count to reduce hash collisions.

Java 9 added another optimization layer: **compact strings**. The backing representation switched from `char[]` (UTF-16, 2 bytes per character) to `byte[]` with an encoding flag. ASCII-only strings use Latin-1 encoding at 1 byte per character — cutting memory consumption in half for the vast majority of strings in typical applications. This applies to both pooled and non-pooled strings automatically.

sections.title: When intern() Helps, When It Hurts, and the G1 Alternative That Needs No Code
sections.content:
Calling `intern()` is a **native JVM call** that acquires a lock on the global string table, walks the bucket chain, and either returns an existing entry or inserts a new one. For small volumes or per-request strings, this synchronization overhead outweighs any memory benefit. The rule is simple: `intern()` is worth it only when the same string value appears thousands of times.

The canonical use case is **parsing repetitive data** — CSV files where column names, status codes, or country codes repeat across millions of rows. Without interning, each parsed row allocates a fresh `"ACTIVE"` string. With interning, all rows share one pooled reference. The memory difference can be gigabytes in data-heavy applications.

The modern alternative that avoids both the locking cost and the code changes is G1 GC's **String Deduplication** (`-XX:+UseStringDeduplication`). It works differently from `intern()` — instead of making String references point to the same pool object, it makes separate String objects share the same **backing `byte[]` array**. Reference identity is preserved (`==` still returns `false`), but the duplicate byte arrays are eliminated. This happens automatically during GC pauses, requires no application code changes, and avoids the global lock contention of `intern()`. For most applications, this is the better choice.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **String pool = shared storage for identical literals** — `"hello" == "hello"` is true; `new String("hello")` bypasses the pool.
- **Java 7 moved pool from PermGen to the main heap** — interned strings became GC-eligible; pre-Java 7 caused PermGen OOM.
- **`intern()` is useful for repetitive values at scale** — status codes, country codes; acquires a global lock, skip on per-request strings.
- **G1's `-XX:+UseStringDeduplication`** — deduplicates the backing `byte[]` during GC without any lock contention or code changes.
- **`new String("hello")` always bypasses the pool** — creates a separate heap object; use `.equals()` for content comparison.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The string pool is how the JVM avoids allocating duplicate objects for identical string literals — when you write `"hello"` twice in source, both references point to the same pool entry.

**How it works:**
- String literals are automatically interned at class loading time
- `"hello" == "hello"` is true because both reference the same pool object
- `new String("hello")` bypasses the pool — `==` against a literal returns false; `.equals()` returns true

**History (PermGen → heap):**
- Before Java 7: pool lived in PermGen — a fixed-size non-GC region; too many interned strings caused `OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space`
- Java 7+: pool moved to the main heap, making interned strings GC-eligible when unreachable

**intern() use case:**
- Useful when parsing millions of rows with repetitive values (status codes, country codes)
- Acquires a global lock on the string table — not worth calling on per-request strings
- Modern alternative: G1's `-XX:+UseStringDeduplication` deduplicates the backing `byte[]` during GC without any lock contention

I recommend `-XX:+UseStringDeduplication` over manual `intern()` for most services — it works without any code changes.
